title: Build a Modern Python API, Worker & Container
subtitle: Use uv, typed requests, async database I/O, a stream queue, tests, and a reproducible non-root image.
analogy: The API is the order counter, the stream is the order rail, the worker prepares the order, and PostgreSQL records the completed receipt. Returning 202 means the order was accepted, not served.
objectives: Explain type hints, validation, async/await, modules, and context managers.
Run the same application as an HTTP API and a background worker.
Trace a JSON request through the queue into PostgreSQL.
Test behavior and build an image from a real uv.lock.
prerequisites: Complete Chapter 1 and copy its pyproject.toml.
Docker is running and ports 5432, 6379 and 8001 are available.

lessons.title: Python fundamentals in the application
body: `class JobRequest(BaseModel)` defines a typed data model. `Field(min_length=1)` adds runtime validation; a plain annotation alone would not do that. Decorators such as `@app.post` and `@broker.task` register functions with a framework.

An async function returns a coroutine. `await` lets the event loop run other work while an asynchronous operation waits. It does not make CPU-heavy Python code parallel. Use a process or job system for expensive CPU work, and never call blocking database/network APIs inside an async handler.

lessons.title: Why both an API and a worker?
body: HTTP requests should not hold a connection open for long-running jobs. The API validates input, queues it, and returns a job ID. A separate worker imports the registered task and writes a result later. This lesson processes text locally; adding an LLM or object-store integration is an extension, not a hidden requirement.

lessons.title: Connections, transactions and migrations
body: The API borrows a pooled connection using `async with`; the worker opens its own connection. Successful transaction contexts commit; failures roll back. Parameterized SQL prevents values from becoming SQL syntax.

Run the initial schema command before starting services. CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS is only an initial migration, not an evolving schema strategy. For later changes adopt versioned migrations, for example Alembic with SQLAlchemy.

lessons.title: Reliability has several layers
body: Stream acknowledgement does not mean exactly-once delivery. Configure retry/reclaim behavior and a dead-letter policy before production; test a worker crash with your broker version. PostgreSQL deduplicates repeats of a particular job ID, but separate retries of POST /enqueue receive different IDs.

This lab also lacks authentication, per-user authorization, rate limits and a transactional outbox. Add those before exposing real customer data. No fixed latency or container-density guarantees are assumed.

handHoldingSteps: Copy the app package, tests, Dockerfile and compose.yaml into the repository root using the exact paths shown. Keep pyproject.toml and uv.lock at that root, not inside app/.
Run Ruff and pytest before starting Docker. The HTTP unit tests mock the queue and do not need a running database.
Run `docker compose up --build -d`. Compose waits for healthy PostgreSQL and Redis, runs the migration, then starts API and worker from the same image.
Open http://localhost:8001/docs. POST a JSON prompt, keep its job_id, then GET /jobs after the simulated work finishes. Follow the worker logs to connect HTTP acceptance to database commit.

For host-side debugging, start only postgres/redis, copy .env.example to .env, run the migration and launch API and worker in separate terminals. Stop any existing container API/worker first so two workers do not consume the same lab stream unexpectedly.
concepts: Lifespan: The startup/shutdown context owns connections; avoid resource creation during import.
Async I/O: await relinquishes the event loop while I/O waits; it does not remove latency or parallelize CPU-bound code.
HTTP contract: 202 means queued, 422 means input validation failed, and 503 means the enqueue attempt failed.
Idempotent persistence: A primary-key conflict can prevent duplicate writes for one job ID; it does not create a distributed exactly-once system.

codeFiles.code: """API and worker share this application package."""
codeFiles.description: Mark app as an importable Python package.

codeFiles.code:
from functools import lru_cache

from psycopg.conninfo import make_conninfo
from pydantic import SecretStr
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict


class Settings(BaseSettings):
    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env", extra="ignore")

    redis_url: str = "redis://localhost:6379/0"
    db_host: str = "localhost"
    db_port: int = 5432
    db_name: str = "appdb"
    db_user: str = "appuser"
    db_password: SecretStr = SecretStr("local-dev-only")
    db_sslmode: str = "disable"  # Local only; AWS sets require.

    @property
    def conninfo(self) -> str:
        # Quote special characters correctly; never log this string.
        return make_conninfo(
            host=self.db_host,
            port=self.db_port,
            dbname=self.db_name,
            user=self.db_user,
            password=self.db_password.get_secret_value(),
            sslmode=self.db_sslmode,
            connect_timeout=5,
        )


@lru_cache
def get_settings() -> Settings:
    return Settings()
codeFiles.description: Typed, environment-driven settings shared by API and worker.

walkthrough.title: Settings(BaseSettings)
walkthrough.explanation: Fields provide types and local defaults. Environment variables override them; SecretStr redacts ordinary representations, but get_secret_value explicitly exposes the value to the database driver.

walkthrough.title: conninfo
walkthrough.explanation: make_conninfo escapes connection fields correctly. This avoids breaking database passwords containing @, : or /. Never log the resulting string.

walkthrough.title: @lru_cache
walkthrough.explanation: Load settings once per process, rather than reading configuration for every request.

codeFiles.code:
from psycopg.rows import dict_row
from psycopg_pool import AsyncConnectionPool

from app.config import get_settings

# Each API process owns its own small pool; construction opens no sockets.
pool = AsyncConnectionPool(
    conninfo=get_settings().conninfo,
    min_size=1,
    max_size=5,
    open=False,
    kwargs={"row_factory": dict_row},
)
codeFiles.description: A small asynchronous connection pool owned by each API process.

walkthrough.title: open=False
walkthrough.explanation: Importing the module performs no network I/O. FastAPI lifespan opens the pool and closes it on shutdown.

walkthrough.title: max_size=5
walkthrough.explanation: Two API processes can use up to ten pooled connections, before worker and migration connections. Scale with the database connection budget in mind.

codeFiles.code:
from taskiq_redis import RedisStreamBroker

from app.config import get_settings

# Streams support acknowledgement; Redis persistence is a separate concern.
broker = RedisStreamBroker(url=get_settings().redis_url)
codeFiles.description: Connect TaskIQ to a Redis-compatible stream broker.

walkthrough.title: RedisStreamBroker
walkthrough.explanation: Streams support acknowledgement. That is different from durable Redis storage, replication and retry/reclaim policy; production systems need all of these considered.

codeFiles.code:
import asyncio
import logging
from uuid import UUID

import psycopg

from app.broker import broker
from app.config import get_settings

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


@broker.task
async def process_ai_job(job_id: str, prompt: str) -> None:
    """A deterministic stand-in for slow external I/O, not an actual LLM call."""
    await asyncio.sleep(2)
    word_count = len(prompt.split())
    # The worker uses its own async connection, not the API's connection pool.
    async with await psycopg.AsyncConnection.connect(get_settings().conninfo) as conn:
        await conn.execute(
            """
            INSERT INTO job_logs (job_id, prompt, word_count)
            VALUES (%s, %s, %s)
            ON CONFLICT (job_id) DO NOTHING
            """,
            (UUID(job_id), prompt, word_count),
        )
    # A successful context exit commits; exceptions cause rollback.
    logger.info("job_completed job_id=%s word_count=%s", job_id, word_count)
codeFiles.description: The background worker turns a prompt into a persisted word-count result.

walkthrough.title: @broker.task
walkthrough.explanation: Registers a Python coroutine as a remotely queued task. Importing app.tasks in the worker registers it with the same broker object.

walkthrough.title: await asyncio.sleep(2)
walkthrough.explanation: Simulates waiting for slow I/O. It is not an LLM call and does not block the event loop like time.sleep would. Real external HTTP calls need an async client, timeouts and error handling.

walkthrough.title: Parameterized SQL
walkthrough.explanation: %s placeholders pass values separately from SQL. ON CONFLICT makes a repeated delivery of the same job_id harmless for this database write; it does not deduplicate two separate HTTP submissions.

codeFiles.description: A typed HTTP API using lifespan instead of deprecated startup event decorators.

walkthrough.title: lifespan
walkthrough.explanation: Open the pool and broker before serving requests; release both on shutdown. The finally blocks also release the pool when broker startup fails.

walkthrough.title: JobRequest and JobAccepted
walkthrough.explanation: Pydantic validates JSON input and documents output in OpenAPI. Empty or oversized prompts produce 422; accepted jobs return 202 because work is unfinished.

walkthrough.title: enqueue
walkthrough.explanation: Generate a stable job ID, await only the enqueue operation, and return without waiting for the slow job. A queue error becomes 503; it is not an acknowledgement of completed work.

walkthrough.title: /health, /ready, /jobs
walkthrough.explanation: Liveness checks the HTTP process; readiness checks PostgreSQL. /jobs queries completed results with an async pooled connection. Readiness does not currently check queue connectivity.

codeFiles.code:
"""One initial, repeatable lab migration; run before starting API or workers."""

import asyncio

import psycopg

from app.config import get_settings


async def main() -> None:
    async with await psycopg.AsyncConnection.connect(get_settings().conninfo) as conn:
        await conn.execute("""
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS job_logs (
                job_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
                prompt TEXT NOT NULL,
                word_count INTEGER NOT NULL,
                created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
            )
        """)
    print("Initial schema ready")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
codeFiles.description: Run the initial SQL schema once as a separate deployment step.

walkthrough.title: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS
walkthrough.explanation: This makes the initial lab setup repeatable. It does not migrate an existing table when columns change; versioned migrations are required as the app evolves.

walkthrough.title: asyncio.run
walkthrough.explanation: A command-line entry point runs the coroutine and waits for it to finish before returning an exit code.

codeFiles.code:
from unittest.mock import AsyncMock

import pytest
from httpx import ASGITransport, AsyncClient

from app.main import app
from app.tasks import process_ai_job

pytestmark = pytest.mark.anyio


@pytest.fixture
def anyio_backend():
    return "asyncio"


@pytest.fixture
async def client(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setattr(process_ai_job, "kiq", AsyncMock())
    # ASGITransport deliberately skips lifespan for isolated HTTP contract tests.
    # Integration tests must exercise real startup, Redis, and PostgreSQL too.
    async with AsyncClient(
        transport=ASGITransport(app=app), base_url="http://test"
    ) as session:
        yield session


async def test_health(client):
    response = await client.get("/health")
    assert response.json() == {"status": "ok"}


async def test_enqueue_returns_202_and_calls_queue(client):
    response = await client.post("/enqueue", json={"prompt": "hello uv"})
    assert response.status_code == 202
    body = response.json()
    assert body["status"] == "queued"
    process_ai_job.kiq.assert_awaited_once_with(body["job_id"], "hello uv")


async def test_empty_prompt_is_rejected(client):
    response = await client.post("/enqueue", json={"prompt": ""})
    assert response.status_code == 422


async def test_queue_outage_is_503(client):
    process_ai_job.kiq.side_effect = ConnectionError("Redis offline")
    response = await client.post("/enqueue", json={"prompt": "hello"})
    assert response.status_code == 503
codeFiles.description: Async HTTP contract tests with HTTPX ASGITransport. They mock the queue and deliberately skip lifespan.

walkthrough.title: AsyncMock
walkthrough.explanation: Assert that valid input calls the queue with the returned job ID. Test invalid input and queue failure separately.

walkthrough.title: Integration boundary
walkthrough.explanation: These tests do not prove Redis, PostgreSQL or lifespan work. The Compose and curl checks below cover the full request-to-result path.

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM python:3.13-slim AS build
COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.6 /uv /usr/local/bin/uv
WORKDIR /workspace
ENV UV_LINK_MODE=copy UV_PYTHON_DOWNLOADS=0
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/uv \
    uv sync --locked --no-dev --no-install-project

FROM python:3.13-slim AS runtime
RUN useradd --create-home --uid 10001 appuser
WORKDIR /workspace
ENV PATH="/workspace/.venv/bin:$PATH" \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
COPY --from=build /workspace/.venv ./.venv
COPY --chown=appuser:appuser app ./app
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
codeFiles.description: Build one locked runtime environment and run the final container as a non-root user.

walkthrough.title: Build stage
walkthrough.explanation: uv sync --locked --no-dev installs only runtime dependencies. Layering the manifest and lockfile before source enables dependency caching.

walkthrough.title: Runtime stage
walkthrough.explanation: Copy the virtual environment and app without uv or development tools. PATH resolves uvicorn/taskiq from that virtual environment.

walkthrough.title: Single image
walkthrough.explanation: ECS and Compose change only the startup command for API, worker or migration. Build and promote the same image digest for all roles.

codeFiles.code:
x-app: &app
  build: .
  image: backend-bootcamp:dev
  environment:
    REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379/0
    DB_HOST: postgres
    DB_PORT: "5432"
    DB_NAME: appdb
    DB_USER: appuser
    DB_PASSWORD: local-dev-only
    DB_SSLMODE: disable

services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:17-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: appuser
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: local-dev-only
      POSTGRES_DB: appdb
    ports: ["127.0.0.1:5432:5432"]
    volumes: ["postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data"]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U appuser -d appdb"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 20
  redis:
    image: redis:7.4-alpine
    command: ["redis-server", "--appendonly", "yes"]
    ports: ["127.0.0.1:6379:6379"]
    volumes: ["redis-data:/data"]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 20
  migrate:
    <<: *app
    command: ["python", "-m", "app.migrate"]
    depends_on:
      postgres: {condition: service_healthy}
  api:
    <<: *app
    ports: ["127.0.0.1:8001:8000"]
    depends_on:
      migrate: {condition: service_completed_successfully}
      redis: {condition: service_healthy}
  worker:
    <<: *app
    command: ["taskiq", "worker", "app.tasks:broker"]
    depends_on:
      migrate: {condition: service_completed_successfully}
      redis: {condition: service_healthy}

volumes:
  postgres-data:
  redis-data:
codeFiles.description: Healthy dependencies, a one-shot migration, then API and worker.

walkthrough.title: Service DNS
walkthrough.explanation: Containers use postgres and redis as hostnames. The host uses localhost through published ports. localhost inside the API container refers to that container, not PostgreSQL.

walkthrough.title: depends_on conditions
walkthrough.explanation: Wait for database health and successful migration before starting API/worker. This controls startup order, not ongoing outage recovery.

walkthrough.title: Ports and volumes
walkthrough.explanation: The API uses host port 8001 to avoid colliding with the course reader on 8000. Named volumes persist data after docker compose down; down -v deletes them.

breakItDrill.title: Stop the worker, keep the API
breakItDrill.scenario: Run `docker compose stop worker`, then submit a valid prompt.
breakItDrill.symptom: The API can return 202, but a new result does not appear until a worker processes the queued job.
breakItDrill.fix: Start the worker again and verify the same job ID reaches PostgreSQL. Do not confuse a queue acceptance response with completion.

assignment.title: Test idempotent persistence
assignment.description: Invoke the registered task twice with the same job_id using a local test script; query the database and explain why only one row is stored. Then explain why repeating an HTTP request is a different case.
assignment.completionHint: Verify the result yourself, then complete the chapter checklist.

recallNote.keyTakeaway: Use typed boundaries, asynchronous I/O, and an explicit lifecycle; keep accepted work separate from completed work.
bullets: Containers share an image, not an event loop or database connection.
Commit uv.lock; build with --locked; keep development dependencies out of runtime.
